title: What an index is
intro: Five short ideas that let you read the S&P 500 figure on every Trendably page without guessing. Read top to bottom; each ends with one question.

concepts.title: What an index measures
read: An index is one number that sums up how a whole group of stocks is doing. Instead of checking 500 prices, you check one.
When the news says “the market fell today”, it almost always means an index fell.
concepts.aside: Think of a class average: it tells you how the class did, not how any one student did.

snapshot.caption: Each name in this strip is an index. The S&P 500 is the one Trendably is built around.

concepts.mistake: An index isn’t something you can own. It’s a measurement, like a temperature reading. To invest in what it tracks, people buy a fund built to copy it — that’s Lesson 3.

question.prompt: A friend says, “The S&P 500 dropped 1% today.” What actually happened?

options.text: Every one of the 500 companies lost about 1%.
options.feedback: An index is a summary. On a day it falls 1%, plenty of its companies can still rise.

options.text: The combined value of a large group of US companies fell by about 1%.
options.feedback: Right. The index sums up the whole group in one number, so a 1% drop describes the group, not each company.

options.text: A company called S&P lost 1% of its value.
options.feedback: S&P is the firm that maintains the index. The index measures other companies, not S&P itself.

options.text: Shares of the S&P 500 in your account are now worth 1% less.
options.feedback: You can’t hold the index itself. You can hold a fund that copies it, which comes later in this chapter.

concepts.title: What the S&P 500 represents
read: The S&P 500 follows about 500 of the largest companies listed in the United States. Together they make up roughly 80% of the value of the whole US stock market, which is why it’s the usual stand-in for “the market”.
A committee chooses the members using rules about size, profits and how easily the shares trade, and swaps companies in and out over time.

snapshot.caption: Every sector and stock you open in the Grid is a slice of the S&P 500.

concepts.mistake: It isn’t simply “the 500 biggest companies”, and it isn’t the whole economy. Private companies, smaller companies and most foreign ones aren’t in it.

question.prompt: A well-known private company, not listed on any stock exchange, doubles in value. What happens to the S&P 500?

options.text: It rises, since the index follows the US economy.
options.feedback: The index follows large listed companies, not the economy as a whole. A private company isn’t part of it.

options.text: It rises, because fast-growing companies are added automatically.
options.feedback: Changes are made by a committee under set rules, and a company has to be publicly listed to qualify.

options.text: Nothing directly — only companies whose shares trade publicly are in the index.
options.feedback: Right. A company has to be listed, and chosen, before its value can move the index.

explore: How does a company get added or removed?
Is the S&P 500 the same as the Dow?

concepts.title: Why big companies count more
read: Companies don’t all count the same. Each one counts in proportion to its market value: share price times the number of shares. This is called market-cap weighting.

A company worth $3 trillion moves the index far more than one worth $30 billion. Group them by sector and it shows clearly: Information Technology alone is about {{sector:Information Technology.weight}}% of the S&P 500.

snapshot.caption: Each bar is a sector’s share of the index. The top two sectors carry {{top2.weight}}% of it.

concepts.mistake: A big jump in a small company barely registers. A small move in a giant can move the whole index.

question.prompt: Two companies each rise 10% today. One is worth $2 trillion, the other $20 billion. Which nudges the S&P 500 more?

options.text: Both the same — they rose by the same percentage.
options.feedback: That would be true if every company counted equally. In the S&P 500, bigger companies carry more weight.

options.text: The $2 trillion company — it carries about a hundred times more weight.
options.feedback: Right. Same percentage move, but a hundred times the weight, so a hundred times the effect on the index.

options.text: The smaller one, because small companies swing the index more.
options.feedback: Small companies often swing more themselves, but their weight is tiny, so their effect on the index is small.

explore: Are there indexes where every company counts equally?

concepts.title: Points and percent
read: Index moves are reported two ways: in points, the change in the number itself, and in percent.

Points depend on how high the index already is, so they’re hard to compare over time. Percent is the fair comparison. A 60-point fall is about 1% with the index near 6,000, but was about 15% in the early 1990s, when the index sat near 400.

snapshot.where: Stock Detail and Market Weather · index quote
snapshot.caption: Across Trendably, moves are shown in percent so different days can be compared fairly.

concepts.mistake: Headlines like “biggest point drop ever” can sound worse than they are. Check the percent before reacting.

question.prompt: Day A: the index falls 40 points from 2,000. Day B: it falls 60 points from 6,000. Which was the bigger move?

options.text: Day B — it lost more points.
options.feedback: More points, but from a much higher level. 60 out of 6,000 is 1%.
Work out each as a share of where the index started: 40 of 2,000 versus 60 of 6,000.

options.text: Day A — it fell about 2%, twice as much as Day B.
options.feedback: Right. 40 out of 2,000 is 2%; 60 out of 6,000 is 1%. Fewer points, bigger move.

explore: Why is the index number itself so high?
How do I work out a percent change?

concepts.title: One number, many different days
read: Because an index is a weighted total, it can hide a lot. Today the S&P 500 moved {{index.moveSigned}}%, yet some sectors rose while others fell harder.
In today’s data, {{best.name}} moved {{best.moveSigned}}% while {{largest.name}} moved {{largest.moveSigned}}%. Because {{largest.name}} is the largest sector, its move weighs most on the index.

snapshot.caption: {{count.down}} sectors fell and {{count.up}} rose, yet the single number at the bottom is all most headlines report.

concepts.mistake: “The market was down” doesn’t mean your stock was down. Look beneath the index before drawing conclusions.

question.prompt: The index closes slightly lower. What can you safely conclude?

options.text: The weighted total of its companies fell — individual stocks and sectors may still have risen.
options.feedback: Right. That’s all one index number can tell you; the detail lives underneath it.

options.text: Most of the companies in it fell.
options.feedback: Not necessarily. A few very large companies falling can outweigh many smaller ones rising.

options.text: Every sector fell, just by different amounts.
options.feedback: Sectors can move in opposite directions on the same day, as the snapshot above shows.

explore: Where in Trendably do I look beneath the index?
Can the index rise while most stocks fall?

recap: An index is one number that summarises a group of stocks. It’s a measurement, not something you own.
The S&P 500 covers about 500 large US-listed companies, roughly 80% of US market value.
Bigger companies count more, in proportion to their market value.
Compare index moves in percent, not points.
One index number can hide very different moves underneath.
